Setting

(i) Population based series of breast cancer cases (ABC study): Women diagnosed with breast cancer at < 55 years age identified through the Anglican Cancer Registry

UK families with multiple breast cancer cases (‘B families’): Families containing two or more breast cancer cases, at least one of which was diagnosed under age 50 years ascertained in response to national publicity in the UK and by referral by oncologists or general practitioners.

characteristics.name: Predictors
characteristics.value:
Predictors

  • Multi-generational family history of cancer including age of onset of breast or ovarian cancer, BRCA mutation status

Measurement of predictors

  • ABC study: Most predictors measured by epidemiological questionnaire (self-reported) including questions on family history, reproductive history (menarche, pregnancies, menopause), oral contraceptive pill and hormone replacement therapy use, past medical history and previous examination of the breast by mammography. The family history included details of all first-degree relatives to include date and place of birth, date of death, and any history of cancer. Details of any other relatives known by the case to have had cancer were also ascertained. BRCA 1/2 mutation status (of index case) measured using Genomic DNA, extracted from blood. Participants were screened for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations by Conformation Sensitive Gel Electrophoresis (CSGE), and mutations were confirmed by sequencing.
  • B families: unclear for family history of cancer predictors, stated “Cancer occurrence and follow up was recorded on all family members”. BRCA 1/2 mutation status measured using Genomic DNA, extracted from blood. Participants were screened for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations by CSGE. Mutation testing was first performed on an index affected individual. If a mutation was found, other relatives were then screened for the same mutation.

Timing of predictor measurement

  • ABC study: at least 3 months after the initial breast cancer diagnosis
  • B families: not reported

characteristics.name: Analysis
characteristics.value:
Sample size

ABC study: 1484 participants/1484 events (case-only)

B Families: 156 families (# individuals not reported)/ 618 events

Model Development (modelling method, method for selection of predictors)

  • Complex segregation analysis used to estimate simultaneous effects of BRCA1, BRCA2, a third hypothetical gene ‘BRCA3’, and a polygenic effect. The hypergeometric polygenic model (HPM) was used to approximate polygenic inheritance and the effect of risk modifiers. Maximum likelihood estimation was used to estimate the parameters.For the ABC families the conditional likelihood of observing the disease phenotypes and mutation status was maximized given the disease phenotype of the index case. For the ‘B’ families, the authors conditioned on the disease phenotypes of all family members. Several models were fitted to data. The goodness of fit of the models was tested using likelihood based tests. Parameters were selected by testing if the addition of parameters to a ‘sporadic’ model (where only the effects of BRCA1 and BRCA2 were considered) improved the fit significantly. The models were constructed by adding parameters that were significant in a stepwise fashion. Non-nested models were compared using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), The best fitting model that minimised the AIC (the polygenic model) was chosen as the final model.

Model validation

  • Not reported for BC occurrence (reported only for prediction of BRCA mutations)

Setting

Women aged 35-50 recruited to one of 10 prospective cohort studies who had never used hormone therapy and were not current users of oral contraceptives. Of these, only women from subgroup analysis with ≥1 BC affected first degree relative applicable for this review.

characteristics.name: Predictors
characteristics.value:
Predictors

  • Gail model predictors (with the exception of atypical hyperplasia which was unavailable)
  • For update, Gail model predictors, serum AMH, total testosterone

Measurement of predictors

GAIL model predictors: Method of measurement of predictors not explicitly stated but likely self-reported by participants within each cohort.

AMH: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) was measured in serum or plasma samples from women who were premenopausal at the time of blood donation using the picoAMH assay (ANSH laboratories). Women who had AMH concentrations below the lowest detectable value (LDV) (< 10% of samples for eight cohorts and < 20% for the remaining two cohorts) were classified into the lowest quartile for analyses. Because it has previously been shown that postmenopausal women have AMH concentrations below the LDV, AMH was not measured in postmenopausal women (23 cases and 40 controls). These participants were classified into the lowest quartile.

Total testosterone: was measured for all subjects in' and for the matched sets for which it was not measured previously for the other cohorts. Measurements were done in the Immunochemical Core Laboratory of the Mayo Clinic by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS).

Timing of predictor measurement

  • Data collected closest to blood draw were used. Data on subsequent age at menopause were also obtained (except for CSB and NSMSC cohorts which did not send follow-up questionnaires).

calibration in the presence of independent right-censoring. This method entailed replacing the single null hypothesis of agreement between true and assigned outcome probabilities for all individuals in the population by the joint null hypothesis that the model-specified event-specific hazards agree with the actual hazards governing events in the population during the risk period.

Sample size

Model Development (modelling method, method for selection of predictors)

  • Authors used a novel Fixed-Stratified method, which allows integration of a new factor into an existing model based on co-estimation of only the correlated sub-components. They used this method to combine a polygenic risk score (PRS) with version 7.02 of the Tyrer-Cuzick breast cancer risk prediction model byattenuating PRS after fixing the effects of confounded factors from the Tyrer-Cuzick model and to constrain risk separately within strata of the confounders.According to standard theory, risks conferred by Tyrer-Cuzick factors that are not correlated with PRS should remain unchanged after incorporation of PRS into the model. The authors therefore focused on the only Tyrer-Cuzick factor which showed correlation with PRS ie. family history of breast cancer.

Model validation

  • Validation 1=Internal validation of CRS : “Clinical testing cohort data were subdivided according to successive time intervals to ensure the independence of development and validation activities” Validation 2 =External validation of CRS “a consecutive series of women who presented to four breast cancer screening centers (Elizabeth Wende Breast Care, The Breast Center of NWA, Bethesda Health, and Cuda Women's Health Center/Cape Cod Healthcare) were prospectively recruited between February 6, 2017 and November 11, 2017 (N = 518)”
  • External validation of TC model (geographical, different setting (women undergoing genetic testing), different investigators)

Model performance measures assessed

  • Calibration

Calibration not measured directly.

Primary analyses tested the CRS and Tyrer-Cuzick individually for association with breast cancer in age-adjusted logistic regression models. Secondary analyses tested the incremental improvement of the CRS over Tyrer-Cuzick by including both risk estimators in the same age-adjusted model. Exploratory analyses tested calibration of the CRS by comparing average absolute risk estimates with those from the Tyrer-Cuzick model; with proper calibration, authors expected to observe the same average risk for Tyrer-Cuzick as for the CRS among unaffected controls. These analyses were conducted separately for Remaining Lifetime Risk (RLR) and 5-year risk of developing breast cancer.

  • Discrimination

Odds Ratio (95% CI)

Discriminatory accuracy of CRS over Tyrer-Cuzick or PRS alone was assessed in validation 1 and validation 2. CRS, Tyrer-Cuzick, and PRS were evaluated separately in terms of likelihood ratio chi-squared test statistics from age-adjusted logistic regression models.

  • Classification

The clinical performance population (N = 32,576) was used to assess risk stratification using the CRS. Remaining Lifetime Risk (RLR) of breast cancer was calculated according to both the Tyrer-Cuzick model and the CRS, and classifications (increased [>20%] or low [≤ 20%] risk) from both were compared.

Some missing data on atypical hyperplasia (48.37%), benign breast conditions, BMI at time of mammogram, number of biopsy examinations (15.22%), menopause status. If yes, how was missing data handled?

Model Development (modelling method, method for selection of predictors)

The model predicts the probability, based on family history, that a woman is a carrier of either a BRCA1 mutation or a BRCA2 mutation and the probability of disease outcome, given predicted genetic status

  • Model developed using Bayesian methods to incorporate all relevant family history, up to second-degree relatives.
  • Mutation frequencies and cancer rates for both carriers and non-carriers of mutations were obtained from published empirical studies
  • Uncertainty in the inputs about family members’ genetic status and the uncertainty about the prevalence of the mutation in the population and about the cancer rates for carriers was incorporated using a Bayesian approach
  • A likelihood ratio for the observed family history is computed. An estimate of the mutation frequency in the population provides the probability of a mutation in the counseland, prior to the ascertainment of family history. Bayes’s rule is applied to determine the probability of a mutation, given family history.
  • Uncertainty about the model parameters is addressed by use of a Monte Carlo simulation

  • The probability that an individual will develop breast cancer or ovarian cancer later in life is calculated as a weighted average of the corresponding probabilities for carriers and non-carriers, when the posterior probabilities of being a carrier and a non-carrier are used as weights.

Model Assumptions:

  • Assume that individuals inherit two BRCA1/BRCA2 alleles, one from each parent, and that alleles are either normal or mutated; mutations are inherited independently.
  • Assume an autosomal dominant inheritance of mutations, empirically supported by the analysis presented Claus et al. (1991)
  • Assume that the shape of the penetrance function for male BRCA2 carriers is the same as that for female BRCA2 carries but that it has a smaller asymptote. Penetrance functions for male BRCA1 carriers are assumed to be the same as those for normal individuals
  • When considering the possibility that an individual may carry mutations at both BRCA1 and BRCA2 their penetrance functions are determined as the cumulative distribution of the minimum of two in dependent events: cancer due to BRCA1 and cancer due to BRCA2.
  • Rates for bilateral recurrences are approximated by assuming that the observed breast cancer rates represent the distribution of the minimum of two independent events: cancer in the left breast and cancer in the right breast.
  • The model considers BRCA1 and BRCA2 only and regards all other breast cancer as being sporadic

Model Development (modelling method, method for selection of predictors)

  • Employed segregation analysis techniques based on Bayes theorem to predict genetic risk from family history factors.
  • Modelling Method: A multi-step approach was used to develop the model:
  1. Breast (& ovarian) cancer risk for the national (UK) population were obtained- incidence rates for general population taken from UK national statistics. Incidence rates for BRCA1/2 mutation carriers taken from published data (Ford et al, Peto et al). Once the risk for the BRCA carriers had been calculated, the risk for a non-BRCA carrier was computed so that the population risk would be the same as the national population.
  2. Modelling the risk with respect to family history- used paper by Anderson et al to model risks of breast cancer for different types of family history.
  3. Calculating the risks for a particular age and genotype - A proportional hazards model to the development of breast cancer was taken for the hypothetical susceptibility gene. It was assumed that this gene increased the risk of breast cancer by the same relative rate for women with and without a BRCA gene, but that it had no influence on ovarian cancer risk. It was also assumed that the susceptibility gene was dominant, so that the risks for a heterozygous woman would be the same as for a homozygous woman with the susceptibility gene. Defined ‘absolute risk’ to mean the chance of getting breast cancer by a certain age, ignoring competing causes of mortality. To calculate the absolute risks over age for the different genotypes calculated the survivor function.
  4. A dominant model was eventually chosen for reasons of simplicity and because it did not overestimate the risk caused by two affected first-degree relatives. The approach taken was to use a two locus genetic model with one of the genes based on BRCA1 and BRCA2, and the other (the low penetrance gene) chosen to give as good a fit as possible to the observed risk from family history. The ‘low penetrance’ gene was assumed to be dominant, so that the risks associated with this gene were the same for women with one or two copies. To do this information from the paper by Anderson et al. was used.
